summary: Principal shrine of Yaha Mogi, the great mother goddess of the region's tribal communities, its annual fair draws lakhs to Sagbara.
description:
Devmogra, near Sagbara in the district's south-east corner, is the spiritual centre of gravity for the Vasava, Bhil and Tadvi communities of the Gujarat–Maharashtra–Madhya Pradesh tri-border: the shrine of Yaha Mogi (Devmogra Mata), the mother goddess whose annual fair transforms these quiet hills into one of western India's largest tribal gatherings. Families arrive on foot, by tractor and truck, carrying offerings of grain and bamboo baskets; vows are fulfilled, marriages blessed, harvests dedicated.

The main fair runs around Mahashivratri (dates follow the lunar calendar) across several days, an extraordinary spectacle of devotion, music and market, and also dense crowds, basic facilities and long queues. Outside fair season the temple is calm: a working shrine where the goddess sits with her granary, and where respectful visitors get an unforced look at living adivasi devotion.

Visit as a guest, not a spectator: photograph people only with clear consent, dress plainly, and buy from the local stalls, that is the economy the fair exists to feed.
highlights: Principal shrine of Yaha Mogi / Devmogra Mata
Annual fair around Mahashivratri drawing lakhs
Calm, welcoming shrine outside fair days
history_legend: Yaha Mogi is the great mother of the region's adivasi cosmology, provider of grain and protector of the community; her granary sits beside her in the shrine. Oral tradition, not text, carries her story, and the annual pilgrimage predates every modern boundary drawn around these hills.

attributes.main_festival: Five-day annual fair ending the day before Mahashivratri (Feb–Mar), with the Gadh Yatra procession

modes.road: Via Sagbara from the Rajpipla–Dediapada corridor; fair days bring managed one-way routes

access.last_mile: Walk from parking to the shrine; fair days mean long approach queues

parking.notes: Large open grounds; managed during the fair

timings.note: Indicative; fair days run extended schedules

visit.notes: The fair runs five days, from Maha Vad Amas to the day before Mahashivratri (Feb–Mar), drawing around five lakh devotees from Gujarat, Maharashtra, MP and Rajasthan; the Gadh Yatra procession is its climax. Plan deliberately for it or deliberately around it.

seasonality.notes: The Mahashivratri-season fair is the peak experience and the peak logistics challenge; ordinary winter days are serene.

experience.photography_notes: During the fair, ask before every people-shot. Offerings and rituals are personal. The granary shrine itself is usually off-limits to cameras.

amenities.food: Stalls and bhojan arrangements, expanding hugely at fair time; Sagbara town otherwise
amenities.guides: Local youths orient visitors; Vasavi and Gujarati are the languages of the ground

warnings: Fair crowds are immense: fix meeting points and keep children in hand
Respect ritual spaces; some inner areas are for community members

tips: For the fair, arrive early morning and expect to walk kilometres
Off-season, combine with the Dediapada belt for a full eastern loop
Buy baskets and produce at the stalls: it is the right kind of souvenir

faqs.q: Can non-tribal visitors attend the fair?
faqs.a: Yes. It is open and welcoming, but you are a guest at someone else's most important gathering. Dress plainly, ask before photographing, and follow stewards' directions.

seo.meta_description: Yaha Mogi's shrine at Devmogra: the great tribal fair near Mahashivratri, respectful-visit notes and access from Rajpipla.
